adults.title: Turning toward the Savior's Lift
adults.big_idea: Jesus Christ loves to lift, and we stay in His lift by noticing the feelings of the Holy Spirit, turning away from what pulls us down, and continuing to turn toward Him.
adults.objective: Learners will name one practice that brings them spiritual lift, recognize one place where they may be slowly drifting, and choose one way this week to turn toward the Savior.
prepare: Read Elder Kearon's talk, especially the sections on sink, on descending without noticing, and on what living in lift looks like.
Bring paper and pens for everyone.
Write two words on the board, far apart: LIFT on the left and SINK on the right.
Mark Matthew 14:28–31, Mark 9:17–27 and 3 Nephi 27:22 in your scriptures.
Pray by name for the people you will teach, and think of one time the Savior lifted you that you could share in a minute or less.

segments.name: Begin: a glider and a question
steps: Open with prayer. If you sing, choose one of the suggested hymns.

In about one minute, tell Elder Kearon's story in your own words: as a teenager he learned to fly a glider with the Royal Air Force, a light aircraft with long wings and no engine. A glider climbs only by finding rising air, which pilots call lift. It loses height in sinking air, which they call sink. Neither can be seen, but both can be felt.
Explain that years later he saw the same pattern in his life with God: we need to avoid sink and find lift.
Hand out paper. Give two quiet minutes for each person to write an answer to the first question below. Tell them no one will be asked to read theirs aloud.
questions: When have you felt clearly lifted toward Heavenly Father? Where were you, and how did it feel?

segments.name: Discover: the Savior's hand
steps: Divide the class in two. One half reads Matthew 14:28–31; the other reads Mark 9:17–27. Ask each to look for three things: how far the person had sunk, what that person or the father said to Jesus, and exactly what the Savior did with His hand.
After three minutes, have one person from each half report in a few sentences.
Read the first key quote aloud (the Savior sought out the most desperate souls and wants to lift you).
Ask the questions below. Wait through the silence; let several people answer before you add anything.
questions: In both accounts, what did the person bring to the Savior, and what did the Savior supply?
What does it change for you to believe that He loves to lift, and not only that He is able to?

segments.name: Go deeper: descending without noticing
steps: Explain Elder Kearon's uncomfortable fact about gliding: a pilot who is not actively climbing in lift is descending, and the descent can be so gradual that it goes unnoticed unless the pilot watches the altitude.
Read the second key quote aloud (how easily we slip from spiritual heights).
Ask people to turn to one neighbor and discuss the first question below for three minutes. Each person should have a turn.
Then give one quiet minute for a private altitude check on their paper: one place where I may be drifting lower without having meant to. Make clear this is between them and the Lord.

Read the first aligned quote (Elder Dube) so that the check ends in hope, not discouragement. Remind the class of Elder Kearon's assurance that when we sink, the gentle Savior is there to lift us as we turn to Him.
questions: Think of a season when you felt close to God. What practices brought you there, and what has happened to those practices since?
Why is a slow drift harder to notice than a sudden fall?

segments.name: Apply: what living in lift looks like
steps: Read the third key quote aloud, and add Elder Kearon's next counsel: when you find lift yourself, show someone else where and how to rise. Write the five simple things under LIFT on the board in short form: find a faithful guide; tune in to the Holy Spirit; join those who are climbing; watch for sink and turn away; show someone else how to rise.
Form groups of three or four and assign each group one of the five. Give them three minutes to answer: what would this look like on an ordinary Tuesday for someone in our ward?
Have each group give one concrete example in a sentence or two. Write a word or two from each beside its line on the board.

Point out Elder Kearon's counsel to notice two kinds of feelings: the sweet, peaceful ones that come with choosing lift, and the dim and dampening ones that lead away from the Redeemer. Ask the question below.
questions: How have you learned to tell the difference between those two kinds of feelings in your own life?

segments.name: Lift another
steps: Tell the class that glider pilots who find lift often climb together in the same column of rising air, and that Elder Kearon called helping others turn from sink into the lift of Jesus Christ our glorious opportunity.
Read the second aligned quote (President Chibota).
Ask each person to write one name: someone they could quietly help toward the Savior this week. Invite one or two to share what they might do, without naming the person.
questions: Who once showed you where lift was to be found? What did that person actually do?

segments.name: Choose and close
steps: Read 3 Nephi 27:22 together. Explain that Elder Kearon gave this as the Savior's promise: “If ye do these things blessed are ye, for ye shall be lifted up at the last day.”
Read the fourth key quote (none of this is complicated).
Ask each person to circle or write one thing on their paper they will do this week to turn toward the Savior, and to tell the person beside them what it is.
Bear a brief testimony that Jesus Christ lives and loves to lift. Tell the class you will begin next week by asking where they felt lift.

key_quotes.text: Our Saviour constantly sought out the most desperate souls sinking into darkness and dread and lifted them up. And He wants to lift you!
How easy it is to slowly slip from spiritual heights we have worked so hard to climb when we neglect the practices and behaviours that brought us there.

Find a faithful guide and learn from them where lift is found. Actively tune in to the sweet feelings of the Holy Spirit and the things in your life that lead you there. Join those who are climbing. Do what they do. Watch closely for the subtle signs of sink in your own life, and turn away decisively.
None of this is complicated; we simply need to keep turning toward the Saviour, into the source of lift, and keep choosing to rise into the light rather than drift imperceptibly into the shadow.

scriptures.use: Half the class reads it silently, looking for how far Peter had sunk, what he said, and what the Savior did with His hand.
The other half reads it, looking for what the father brought to Jesus and how the account ends for the boy.
Read together at the close as the promise Elder Kearon attached to living in lift.
Optional, if time allows or for home study: read Ammon's words and ask why being lifted by God is so hard to put into words.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Dube
aligned_quotes.text: We do not need to perfect ourselves to come to Christ. We come to Christ to be perfected.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Chibota
aligned_quotes.text: His grace is sufficient to lift you above every label and limitation.

takeaways: Jesus Christ loves to lift, and He wants to lift me.
If I am not climbing toward Him I am slowly descending, so I watch my altitude.
Staying in lift is not complicated: I keep turning toward the Savior.
act: Each evening this week, write one line: where did I feel lift today, and what was I doing?
Choose one practice that once brought you close to God and has slipped, and take it up again for seven days.
Name one quiet source of sink in your week and decide in advance how you will turn away from it.
Reach out to the person whose name you wrote, with a visit, a message or an invitation to come with you.
adapt: At home or with two or three people: skip the groups. Read Matthew 14:28–31 together, do the altitude check quietly, then talk through the five simple things as a family and choose one together.
Large class: keep every discussion in pairs or threes and take only two or three reports each time, so that everyone speaks and you still finish.
Only 15 minutes: do the opening question, the altitude check with the second key quote, and the closing choice with 3 Nephi 27:22.

youth.title: No Engine: Finding Lift
youth.big_idea: The Savior is the source of our lift; we can learn to feel it through the Holy Ghost, turn away from sink, and climb with others.
youth.objective: Youth will be able to describe what spiritual lift and spiritual sink feel like for them and will choose one specific way to turn toward the Savior this week.
prepare: Read Elder Kearon's talk. Be ready to tell his gliding story in about two minutes without notes.
Bring one sheet of plain paper and a pen for each person, plus a few extra sheets.
Clear a space for throwing paper gliders, and mark a starting line on the floor with a book or a strip of paper.
Write the three references on the board: Matthew 14:28–31; Mark 5:35–42; Mark 9:17–27.
Ask the youth to bring their scriptures or have the Gospel Library app ready on their phones.

segments.name: Glider challenge
steps: As youth walk in, hand each a sheet of paper. Say only: you have 90 seconds to build a glider. Longest flight wins.
Line everyone up at the starting line and launch together on a count of three, throwing away from faces. Cheer the winner. Run it a second time if they want a rematch and time allows.
Ask the first question below. Draw out the obvious point: with no engine, every glider started coming down the moment it left a hand.
Open with prayer.
questions: What would a glider with no engine need in order to stay up, or even climb?

segments.name: Elder Kearon in his mid-teens
steps: Tell the story. As a boy at boarding school in England, Elder Kearon watched aeroplanes and dreamed of flying home to his parents, who were thousands of miles away. In his mid-teens he spent part of two summers at an airfield learning to fly a glider with the air force.

Explain the two words he learned. Lift is rising air; a pilot cannot see it but can feel a wing tip upward, and turns toward it. Sink is sinking air; it can feel like falling, and he learned to turn away from it decisively.
Tell them that about ten years later, early in his journey of faith, he saw that the same is true spiritually: we must avoid sink and find lift.
Read the first key quote (the Savior wants to lift you).
questions: Elder Kearon said the most important skill was not seeing lift but feeling it. Why might that matter for how God speaks to us?

segments.name: Three rescues, three minutes
steps: Split into three teams and give each one reference from the board.
Each team has three minutes to read its account and prepare a 30-second report that answers: Who was sinking, and how bad was it? What exactly did Jesus do? One detail most people miss.
Hear the three reports. Keep time with a phone timer and keep it light.
Ask the questions below to the whole group.
questions: What do the three accounts have in common?
None of these people lifted themselves. What does that say to someone who feels too far down?

segments.name: My lift, my sink
steps: Have each person turn their glider paper over, or take a new sheet, and draw a line down the middle: LIFT on one side, SINK on the other. Promise that no one will collect or read these.

Give two quiet minutes. Under LIFT they list places, people, music, habits and moments that leave them feeling peaceful and closer to the Savior. Under SINK they list what leaves them feeling dim, dampened or further from Him. Suggest they glance at the home screen of their phone as they think about both columns.
Explain Elder Kearon's uncomfortable fact: in gliding, if you are not actively climbing you are descending, and it can be so gradual you do not notice unless you watch your altitude.
Discuss the questions below honestly. It is fine to say that learning to recognize the Spirit takes practice. Elder Kearon himself described learning it, the way he learned to feel rising air.
questions: Without sharing anything private: what is one thing on your LIFT side that might surprise the rest of us?
How can you tell the difference between spiritual sink and simply having a hard day?
What would watching your altitude look like for someone your age?

segments.name: Flight plan
steps: Read the second key quote and list the simple things on the board in short form: find a faithful guide; tune in to the Holy Spirit; join those who are climbing; watch for sink and turn away. Then read the third key quote and add: show someone else how to rise.
Read the first aligned quote, in which Sister Muñoz Spannaus shares counsel from President Oaks about friends. Ask how it matches joining those who are climbing.
In pairs, each person picks one of the five and turns it into a plan for this week that is specific enough to check: what, when, and with whom. Partners help each other make it realistic.
Have each person write the plan on the wing of their glider and tell it to their partner.
questions: Who is a faithful guide you actually trust, and what could you ask that person this week?

segments.name: When you sink
steps: Say plainly that everyone in the room, including you, will sink sometimes. Read the second aligned quote (Elder Dube), and remind them of Elder Kearon's words that when we sink, our gentle Savior is there to lift us up as we turn to Him.
Have one youth read 3 Nephi 27:22 aloud. Explain that Elder Kearon gave it as the Savior's promise to those who keep turning toward Him.
Read the fourth key quote slowly (no limit to how high you can climb with Him). Bear your testimony in a sentence or two.
Ask them to keep the glider where they will see it. Tell them that next week you will ask two things: where did you feel lift, and did you do your flight plan?

key_quotes.text: Our Saviour constantly sought out the most desperate souls sinking into darkness and dread and lifted them up. And He wants to lift you!

Find a faithful guide and learn from them where lift is found. Actively tune in to the sweet feelings of the Holy Spirit and the things in your life that lead you there. Join those who are climbing. Do what they do. Watch closely for the subtle signs of sink in your own life, and turn away decisively.
And when you find lift yourself, show someone else where and how to rise! Then soar in the joy of the Lord!
Your Saviour is your lift. He is your ever-rising air. There is no limit to how high you can climb with Him.

scriptures.use: Team one reads it and reports who was sinking, what Jesus did, and one detail most people miss.
Team two reads it and gives the same three-part report.
Team three reads it and gives the same three-part report.
One youth reads it aloud at the end as the promise Elder Kearon quoted.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Dallin H. Oaks, quoted by Sister Muñoz Spannaus
aligned_quotes.text: number seven is an invitation from our prophet, President Dallin H. Oaks: “Seek friends … who are striving to follow the Lord … with whom you can feel the Spirit and … reinforce your faith.”

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Dube
aligned_quotes.text: We do not need to perfect ourselves to come to Christ. We come to Christ to be perfected.

takeaways: The Savior wants to lift me, however far down I feel.
I cannot see spiritual lift, but I can learn to feel it through the Holy Ghost.
When I notice sink, I turn away decisively and turn toward Him.
act: Carry out the flight plan written on your glider, and tell your partner when you have done it.
For three days, before you fall asleep, note on your phone one moment of lift and one moment of sink from that day.
Pick one item from your SINK column and turn away from it for a week; put something from your LIFT column in its place.
Show one friend where you find lift: invite them to an activity, to seminary, or to sit with you at church.
adapt: At home with one or two youth: fold gliders together as a family, read only Matthew 14:28–31, and do the LIFT and SINK page and the flight plan side by side with a parent doing their own.
Large class: run the glider contest in heats of five, and use six teams, two for each scripture account, with one team reporting and the other adding a detail.
Short on time: keep the glider challenge, the LIFT and SINK page and the flight plan; summarize the three rescues yourself in one minute.

children.title: Jesus Loves to Lift Me
children.big_idea: Jesus loves me and wants to lift me up.
children.objective: Children will be able to say that Jesus loves to lift them, tell how He lifted Peter, and choose one way to lift someone else this week.
prepare: Read Matthew 14:28–31 and the part of Elder Kearon's talk about learning to fly a glider.
Bring a blanket, several sheets of paper, and crayons.
Bring a folder or a stiff piece of card to use as a fan.
Clear a space on the floor where children can move safely.

segments.name: Welcome and song
steps: Greet each child by name and invite a child to pray.
Sing the first suggested song together.
Tell the children that today they will learn something Jesus loves to do. Teach the sentence and say it together twice, raising both hands high on the last word: Jesus loves to lift.

segments.name: Fly like a glider
steps: Tell the children that when Elder Kearon was a boy he wanted very much to fly. He learned to fly a glider, which is an aeroplane with long wings and no engine.
Have the children stretch out their arms like wings and glide slowly and quietly around the room, without touching anyone.

Explain that rising air, called lift, carries a glider up. When you call out lift, they glide on tiptoe with wings high. Sinking air, called sink, takes a glider down. When you call out sink, they glide down low, then turn around and rise again.
Call lift and sink several times, then land everyone back in their seats.

segments.name: Air we cannot see
steps: Hold a sheet of paper up high and let go. Ask what happened.
Hold another sheet flat on your open hand, and have a child wave the folder upward beneath it, or blow from below, so the paper lifts and flutters. Let two or three children have a turn.
Ask the first question below. Then read the key quote about rising air: “You cannot see it, but you can see what it does.”
Explain simply: we cannot see Jesus right now, but He is real and He helps us. The Holy Ghost helps us feel His love, like a warm and peaceful feeling inside.
Say together again: Jesus loves to lift.
questions: Could you see the air? How do you know it was there?
When have you felt warm and peaceful inside?

segments.name: Jesus lifts Peter
steps: Spread the blanket on the floor as the sea. Tell the story from Matthew 14:28–31 in a few simple sentences: Peter walked on the water toward Jesus, he became afraid and began to sink, he called to Jesus for help, and straight away Jesus reached out His hand and caught him.
Act it out. One child is Peter and steps onto the blanket, then slowly kneels down as if sinking and calls to Jesus for help. You, or an older child, reach out a hand and gently help Peter stand.
Each time Peter stands, everyone says: Jesus loves to lift.
Repeat until each child who wants a turn has been Peter.
Tell the children Elder Kearon's words about them: “And He wants to lift you!”
questions: What did Peter do when he started to sink?
What can we do when we feel sad or afraid?

segments.name: Draw a time I felt lifted
steps: Give each child paper and crayons.
Ask them to draw a time they felt happy and close to Jesus. Offer ideas: praying, singing a Primary song, being outdoors, helping someone, hearing a scripture story.
Walk around and ask each child to tell you about the drawing. Write the sentence Jesus loves to lift me at the top of each page, or let older children write it themselves.
Use the aligned quote from Elder Fale: say it once, then have the children say it with you.

segments.name: We can help lift
steps: Explain that Elder Kearon said that when we find lift, we can show someone else how to rise. Jesus lets us help Him.
Put the children in pairs. One sits on the floor; the other holds out a hand, says something kind, and gently helps the partner stand. Then they swap.
Ask the question below and take an answer from every child who wants to give one. Suggest ideas if needed: say a kind word, invite someone to play, share a crayon, pray for someone.
questions: How could you help someone feel lifted this week?

segments.name: Choose and close
steps: Ask each child to choose one way to lift someone this week and whisper it to you or to a neighbor.
Say the sentence one more time together, hands high: Jesus loves to lift.
Bear a short testimony that Jesus lives, loves each child, and will help them when they pray.
Send the drawings home. Tell the children that next week you will ask whom they helped lift. Close with the second suggested song or a prayer.

key_quotes.text: And He wants to lift you!
You cannot see it, but you can see what it does.
we have an adoring Father in Heaven, whose Son, our Saviour, loves to lift!

scriptures.use: Tell the story of Peter in simple words and act it out on the blanket; older children can read verse 31 aloud.
With older children, read it aloud and listen for what Jesus promises to do for those who follow Him.
Optional for older children: read it aloud and ask which bird the verse mentions and how that bird moves.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Fale
aligned_quotes.text: I am a child of God and He loves me.

takeaways: Jesus loves me and wants to lift me.
I can help lift someone else.
act: Say a prayer each day and tell Heavenly Father one thing that made you feel happy and peaceful.
Do one kind thing to lift someone: a kind word, an invitation to play, or a helping hand.
Show your drawing to someone at home and tell them how Jesus lifted Peter.
music: I'm Trying to Be like Jesus

adapt.younger: For ages 3–7: keep each part short and repeat the sentence Jesus loves to lift, with hands raised, after every activity. Give the glider game and the Peter story extra turns and let every child be Peter. Shorten the drawing time and have a helper write the sentence on each page. Skip the extra scriptures.
adapt.older: For ages 8–11: have a child read Matthew 14:28–31 aloud before acting it out, and another read 3 Nephi 27:22. Let an older child call lift and sink in the glider game and play the one who reaches out a hand. Ask a harder question: how can you tell when something is lifting you closer to Jesus and when it is pulling you away? On the drawing, have them add one way they will lift someone this week.
